name: Molly E. Brown
statement: Understanding environmental change. Advancing science for human well-being.
summary: Molly E. Brown's research integrates satellite observations, environmental information, socioeconomic data, and interdisciplinary analysis to understand climate-related risks to agriculture, food security, and human well-being. Her work connects Earth science with real-world applications and decision-making.
biography: Molly E. Brown is a Research Professor in the Department of Geographical Sciences at the University of Maryland, College Park. Her research connects satellite observations of the land surface with the economic and social processes that determine whether people have enough to eat — from vegetation dynamics and rainfall across semi-arid Africa to local grain prices, child nutrition and the decisions of humanitarian and agricultural organizations.

Before joining the University of Maryland faculty in 2015, she spent more than a decade at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, first as a senior research scientist with Science Systems and Applications, Inc. and then, from 2008, as a civil servant research scientist. At Goddard she served as a vegetation index specialist responsible for consistent long-term vegetation data records, as liaison and principal investigator working with the US Agency for International Development's Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET), and as lead of the pre-launch applications programs for the Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) and ICESat-2 missions.

She was lead author of the USDA technical report Climate Change, Global Food Security, and the U.S. Food System, prepared as part of the US National Climate Assessment, and is the author of two books: Famine Early Warning Systems and Remote Sensing Data (Springer, 2008) and Food Security, Food Prices and Climate Variability (Earthscan/Routledge, 2014). Since 2015 she has also served as Chief Science Officer of 6th Grain Corporation, guiding geospatial investments in a digital platform for farmers, and from 2020 to 2022 she held a part-time appointment as Professor of Food-based Strategies for Nutrition at the University of Greenwich's Natural Resources Institute.

She earned her PhD in Geography from the University of Maryland in 2002, with a dissertation on the impact of biophysical conditions on food security in three Sahelian countries, advised by Stephen D. Prince. Her path into the field began in Senegal, where she served as a US Peace Corps volunteer and later managed professional education programs in Dakar.
approach: Brown's work follows a chain of evidence that runs from orbit to outcome. Satellite records of vegetation, rainfall, soil moisture, temperature and land cover describe environmental conditions consistently across space and time. Those conditions are then linked — statistically and through models — to agricultural production, market prices, household food access and child health, using survey, price and demographic data that are rarely collected together.

Equally central is the question of use: who needs Earth observations, when, and in what form. Through NASA's mission applications programs, the Carbon Monitoring System and long collaboration with famine early warning analysts, she has studied how scientific data products move into operational decisions, and what makes that transfer succeed.

chain.text: Long-term records of vegetation, rainfall, soil moisture, temperature, elevation and land cover.
Growing-season onset and length, drought, phenology, water availability, cropland extent.
Crop production, local food prices, market integration, livelihoods and trade.
Food access, diet diversity, child stunting and acute malnutrition, health and fertility.
Famine early warning, anticipatory action, index insurance, mission applications and policy.

contributions.title: Long-term vegetation records
contributions.text: Helped produce and distribute the GIMMS 8-km AVHRR NDVI record and evaluated its consistency with MODIS, SPOT-Vegetation, SeaWiFS and Landsat — a foundation for decades of vegetation-change research.

contributions.title: Satellite data in famine early warning
contributions.text: For more than a decade linked NASA vegetation and rainfall observations to USAID's Famine Early Warning Systems Network, and synthesised the field in Famine Early Warning Systems and Remote Sensing Data (2008).

contributions.title: Environment and food prices
contributions.text: Developed spatially explicit price models and food price indices that tie satellite-observed growing conditions and international shocks to local food prices, summarised in Food Security, Food Prices and Climate Variability (2014).

contributions.title: Mission applications programs
contributions.text: Led the pre-launch applications programs for NASA's SMAP and ICESat-2 missions, including Early Adopter programs later recognised with a 2024 NASA Honor Award.

contributions.title: Climate, conflict and child health
contributions.text: Joined satellite climate records with household surveys to study drought, heat and conflict as drivers of child stunting, diet diversity and acute malnutrition.

contributions.title: Climate change and the food system
contributions.text: Led the USDA technical report Climate Change, Global Food Security, and the U.S. Food System for the US National Climate Assessment.
